modules.title: 5.1 Theories of Acids and Bases
modules.html:
An acid was originally defined as a substance that turns blue litmus red, tastes sour, and neutralises bases. As chemistry matured, three progressively wider theories replaced that simple description.

1. Arrhenius theory (1887)

An acid is a substance that ionises in water to produce hydrogen ions, \(H^+\); a base produces hydroxide ions, \(OH^-\).

$$HCl_{(aq)} \rightarrow H^+_{(aq)} + Cl^-_{(aq)} \qquad NaOH_{(aq)} \rightarrow Na^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}$$

The bare proton does not exist alone in water; it attaches to a water molecule to give the hydroxonium ion, \(H_3O^+\). Limitation: the theory only works for aqueous solutions and cannot explain why ammonia (which has no \(OH\) group) is basic.

2. Brønsted–Lowry theory (1923)

An acid is a proton donor; a base is a proton acceptor. Every acid has a conjugate base formed after it loses its proton, and every base has a conjugate acid.

$$\underset{acid}{NH_4^+} + \underset{base}{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \underset{conj.\ base}{NH_3} + \underset{conj.\ acid}{H_3O^+}$$

Substances such as water, \(HCO_3^-\) and \(HSO_4^-\) can donate or accept a proton; they are described as amphiprotic (or amphoteric).

3. Lewis theory (1923)

A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor; a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor. This is the widest definition and explains reactions with no proton at all:

$$BF_3 + :NH_3 \rightarrow F_3B \leftarrow NH_3$$

Here \(BF_3\) has an incomplete octet and accepts the lone pair on nitrogen, forming a dative (coordinate) bond. Metal ions such as \(Cu^{2+}\) and \(Al^{3+}\) are Lewis acids when they form complex ions with water or ammonia ligands.

Strong versus weak

Strength is about the degree of ionisation, not the concentration. A strong acid (HCl, \(HNO_3\), \(H_2SO_4\)) is completely ionised in water; a weak acid (ethanoic acid, carbonic acid, \(H_2S\)) is only partially ionised and sets up an equilibrium:

$$CH_3COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_3COO^- + H^+$$

Strong bases: NaOH, KOH, \(Ba(OH)_2\). Weak bases: \(NH_3\), amines, \(Ca(OH)_2\) (also sparingly soluble). Basicity of an acid is the number of replaceable hydrogen atoms per molecule: HCl is monobasic, \(H_2SO_4\) dibasic, \(H_3PO_4\) tribasic. Acidity of a base is the number of hydroxide ions it can furnish.

Typical reactions of acids

  • Acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen: \(Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2\)
  • Acid + base/oxide → salt + water: \(CuO + 2HCl \rightarrow CuCl_2 + H_2O\)
  • Acid + trioxocarbonate(IV) → salt + water + \(CO_2\): \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

Concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid is additionally a powerful dehydrating agent (it chars sugar) and an oxidising agent, while dilute trioxonitrate(V) acid oxidises copper without releasing hydrogen.

examples.q: Write the conjugate base of \(H_2PO_4^-\) and its conjugate acid.
examples.a: Conjugate base (lose H⁺): \(HPO_4^{2-}\). Conjugate acid (gain H⁺): \(H_3PO_4\). The ion is therefore amphiprotic.

examples.q: Why is ammonia a base under Brønsted–Lowry but not under Arrhenius?
examples.a: Ammonia contains no \(OH\) group so it cannot release hydroxide directly (Arrhenius fails). It does accept a proton from water, \(NH_3+H_2O\rightleftharpoons NH_4^++OH^-\), so it is a Brønsted base.

examples.q: Distinguish between a dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid.
examples.a: Dilute strong acid: few moles per dm³ but fully ionised, so a relatively high [H⁺]. Concentrated weak acid: many moles per dm³ but only slightly ionised. Strength = extent of ionisation; concentration = amount per unit volume.

modules.title: 5.2 The pH Scale, Indicators and Titration
modules.html:
Water self-ionises very slightly:

$$2H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_3O^+ + OH^- \qquad K_w = [H^+][OH^-] = 1\times10^{-14}\ mol^2dm^{-6}\ (25^\circ C)$$

The concentration of \(H^+\) in a solution spans many powers of ten, so Sørensen defined

$$pH = -\log_{10}[H^+] \qquad pOH = -\log_{10}[OH^-] \qquad pH + pOH = 14$$

pHNatureExample
0–3strongly acidicgastric juice, 0.1 M HCl
4–6weakly acidicrain water, vinegar, milk
7neutralpure water at 25°C
8–10weakly alkalinesea water, baking-soda solution
11–14strongly alkaline0.1 M NaOH, oven cleaner

Indicators

An acid–base indicator is a weak organic acid (or base) whose ionised and unionised forms have different colours:

$$HIn \rightleftharpoons H^+ + In^- \quad (\text{colour A} \rightleftharpoons \text{colour B})$$

IndicatorAcid colourAlkaline colourpH range
Methyl orangered/pinkyellow3.1–4.4
Litmusredblue5.0–8.0
Phenolphthaleincolourlesspink8.3–10.0
Bromothymol blueyellowblue6.0–7.6

Choosing an indicator

  • Strong acid + strong base (equivalence pH 7): any indicator — methyl orange or phenolphthalein.
  • Strong acid + weak base (equivalence pH < 7, e.g. HCl vs \(NH_3\)): methyl orange.
  • Weak acid + strong base (equivalence pH > 7, e.g. \(CH_3COOH\) vs NaOH): phenolphthalein.
  • Weak acid + weak base: no sharp change — titration is not practicable; use a conductivity or pH meter.

Volumetric analysis

A standard solution has accurately known concentration and is prepared from a primary standard (anhydrous \(Na_2CO_3\), \(KHC_8H_4O_4\), oxalic acid) which is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic and of high molar mass. NaOH and HCl are not primary standards.

The titration formula:

$$\frac{C_AV_A}{C_BV_B}=\frac{n_A}{n_B}$$

where \(n_A\) and \(n_B\) are the stoichiometric coefficients of acid and base in the balanced equation.

Apparatus: pipette (delivers a fixed volume of the solution in the conical flask), burette (delivers variable volume, read to 0.05 cm³), conical flask (swirled without loss), white tile (to see the end-point). Concordant titres are readings within 0.10–0.20 cm³ of one another; only these are averaged.

examples.q: Calculate the pH of 0.005 mol dm⁻³ \(H_2SO_4\), assuming full ionisation.
25.0 cm³ of NaOH needed 22.5 cm³ of 0.100 M \(H_2SO_4\). Find the concentration of the alkali.
Why is phenolphthalein unsuitable for titrating ammonia solution with hydrochloric acid?
examples.a: The salt formed, \(NH_4Cl\), hydrolyses to give an acidic end-point (pH about 5). Phenolphthalein changes over pH 8.3–10.0, well above that, so it would change colour long before the true equivalence point. Methyl orange (3.1–4.4) is used.

modules.title: 5.3 Salts: Types, Preparation and Properties
modules.html:
A salt is the compound formed when the replaceable hydrogen of an acid is wholly or partly replaced by a metal or by the ammonium ion.

Types of salt

  • Normal salt — all replaceable H replaced: NaCl, \(Na_2SO_4\), \((NH_4)_2SO_4\).
  • Acid salt — only part of the H replaced; only dibasic/tribasic acids form them: \(NaHSO_4\), \(NaHCO_3\), \(Na_2HPO_4\).
  • Basic salt — contains \(OH\) or \(O\) in addition to the anion: \(Pb(OH)Cl\), \(Mg(OH)Cl\), \(Cu(OH)_2\!\cdot\!CuCO_3\) (malachite).
  • Double salt — two simple salts crystallised together, ionising into all the constituent ions: \(KAl(SO_4)_2\!\cdot\!12H_2O\) (alum), \((NH_4)_2SO_4\!\cdot\!FeSO_4\!\cdot\!6H_2O\) (Mohr's salt).
  • Complex salt — contains a complex ion that does not break down: \(K_4[Fe(CN)_6]\), \([Cu(NH_3)_4]SO_4\).

Methods of preparation

MethodSuitable forExample
Acid + metalsoluble salts of moderately reactive metals (Zn, Fe, Mg)\(Mg+H_2SO_4\rightarrow MgSO_4+H_2\)
Acid + insoluble base/carbonatesoluble salts of unreactive metals (Cu, Pb)\(CuO+H_2SO_4\rightarrow CuSO_4+H_2O\)
Titration (acid + alkali)soluble salts of Na, K, \(NH_4^+\)\(NaOH+HCl\rightarrow NaCl+H_2O\)
Precipitation (double decomposition)insoluble salts\(AgNO_3+NaCl\rightarrow AgCl\!\downarrow+NaNO_3\)
Direct combinationanhydrous salts of variable-valency metals\(2Fe+3Cl_2\rightarrow 2FeCl_3\)

Solubility rules (learn these)

  • All trioxonitrates(V), and all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts, are soluble.
  • All chlorides are soluble except \(AgCl\), \(PbCl_2\) (soluble in hot water) and \(Hg_2Cl_2\).
  • All tetraoxosulphates(VI) are soluble except \(BaSO_4\), \(PbSO_4\) and \(CaSO_4\) (slightly soluble).
  • All trioxocarbonates(IV) are insoluble except those of Na, K and \(NH_4^+\).

Water of crystallisation and related behaviour

  • Hydrated salt: contains water of crystallisation, e.g. \(CuSO_4\!\cdot\!5H_2O\) (blue), \(Na_2CO_3\!\cdot\!10H_2O\). Heating drives the water off, leaving the anhydrous salt (white \(CuSO_4\)) — a reversible physical test for water.
  • Efflorescence: a hydrated salt loses water to the atmosphere and crumbles to powder, e.g. \(Na_2CO_3\!\cdot\!10H_2O\), \(FeSO_4\!\cdot\!7H_2O\).
  • Deliquescence: a solid absorbs so much moisture that it dissolves in it, e.g. NaOH, \(CaCl_2\), \(MgCl_2\).
  • Hygroscopy: absorbs moisture but does not dissolve, e.g. conc. \(H_2SO_4\), CuO, \(P_4O_{10}\); used as drying agents.

Salt hydrolysis

Not every salt solution is neutral. A salt of a strong acid and weak base (\(NH_4Cl\), \(AlCl_3\)) hydrolyses to give an acidic solution; a salt of a weak acid and strong base (\(CH_3COONa\), \(Na_2CO_3\)) gives an alkaline solution; a salt of a strong acid and strong base (NaCl, \(KNO_3\)) is neutral.

examples.q: Which method would you use to prepare lead(II) chloride and why?
examples.a: Precipitation: \(Pb(NO_3)_2+2NaCl\rightarrow PbCl_2\downarrow+2NaNO_3\). \(PbCl_2\) is insoluble in cold water, so it cannot be crystallised from a titration or metal–acid route (lead also becomes coated and the reaction stops).

examples.q: Explain why a solution of \(Na_2CO_3\) turns red litmus blue.
examples.a: It is the salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (\(H_2CO_3\)). The carbonate ion hydrolyses: \(CO_3^{2-}+H_2O\rightleftharpoons HCO_3^-+OH^-\), giving excess hydroxide and an alkaline solution.

examples.q: 2.86 g of \(Na_2CO_3\cdot10H_2O\) was heated to constant mass, leaving 1.06 g. Show that the formula is consistent.
examples.a: Mass of water lost = 1.80 g = 0.10 mol. Moles \(Na_2CO_3\)=1.06/106=0.01 mol. Ratio salt:water = 0.01:0.10 = 1:10, confirming the decahydrate.

modules.title: 5.4 Acid Rain, Buffers and Everyday Applications
modules.html:
Buffer solutions resist change in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added. An acidic buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its salt (ethanoic acid + sodium ethanoate); a basic buffer is a weak base and its salt (ammonia + ammonium chloride).

When acid is added: \(CH_3COO^- + H^+ \rightarrow CH_3COOH\) — the added protons are mopped up. When alkali is added: \(CH_3COOH + OH^- \rightarrow CH_3COO^- + H_2O\). Blood is buffered near pH 7.4 by the \(H_2CO_3/HCO_3^-\) system; a deviation of even 0.4 pH units is life-threatening.

Acid rain

Unpolluted rain is already slightly acidic (pH ~5.6) because dissolved \(CO_2\) forms carbonic acid. Acid rain (pH below 5) comes from oxides of sulphur and nitrogen released by burning fossil fuels and by vehicle engines:

$$SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3 \qquad 2SO_2+O_2 \rightarrow 2SO_3 \qquad SO_3+H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_4$$

$$4NO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4HNO_3$$

Effects: corrosion of limestone and marble buildings, leaching of nutrients from soil, killing of fish in lakes (aluminium ions mobilised), damage to leaves and to metal roofing sheets. Control: flue-gas desulphurisation with \(CaO\), catalytic converters, low-sulphur fuels, liming of affected lakes.

Industrial and domestic uses

  • \(H_2SO_4\) — fertilisers, car batteries, detergents, dyes, drying agent.
  • \(HNO_3\) — fertilisers (\(NH_4NO_3\)), explosives, dyes.
  • NaOH — soap and paper making, refining bauxite.
  • \(NaHCO_3\) — baking powder, antacid, fire extinguishers.
  • \(Ca(OH)_2\) — neutralising acidic soil, mortar, water treatment.
  • NaCl — food, and raw material for the chlor-alkali industry.

Testing for ions in the laboratory

IonTestObservation
\(CO_3^{2-}\)add dilute HCleffervescence; gas turns lime water milky
\(SO_4^{2-}\)\(BaCl_2\) + dilute HClwhite precipitate insoluble in acid
\(Cl^-\)\(AgNO_3\) + dilute \(HNO_3\)white precipitate, soluble in \(NH_3\)
\(NH_4^+\)warm with NaOHpungent gas turning damp red litmus blue
\(Fe^{2+}\)NaOHdirty-green precipitate
\(Fe^{3+}\)NaOHreddish-brown precipitate

examples.q: Why does rain in an industrial city have a lower pH than rain in a rural area?
examples.a: Industrial air contains \(SO_2\) and \(NO_2\) from burning fossil fuels. These dissolve and are oxidised to \(H_2SO_4\) and \(HNO_3\), strong acids that lower the pH well below the natural 5.6 caused by dissolved \(CO_2\).

examples.q: Explain, with equations, how a \(CH_3COOH/CH_3COONa\) buffer resists added NaOH.
examples.a: The weak acid neutralises the added hydroxide: \(CH_3COOH+OH^-\rightarrow CH_3COO^-+H_2O\). Because a large reservoir of undissociated acid remains, \([H^+]\) and hence pH barely change.

examples.q: Two white solids A and B: A effervesces with dilute HCl; B gives a white precipitate with \(BaCl_2\)/HCl. Identify the anions.
examples.a: A contains \(CO_3^{2-}\) (the gas turns lime water milky). B contains \(SO_4^{2-}\) (white \(BaSO_4\) insoluble in acid).

quiz.q: According to Arrhenius, an acid produces which ion in aqueous solution?
quiz.solution: Arrhenius acids ionise in water to give hydrogen ions.

quiz.q: A Brønsted–Lowry base is defined as a
quiz.solution: Brønsted bases accept protons; Lewis bases donate electron pairs.

quiz.q: A Lewis acid is best described as
options: a substance that turns litmus blue
quiz.solution: Lewis acids accept a lone pair, e.g. BF₃.

quiz.q: The conjugate base of \(H_2SO_4\) is
quiz.solution: Removing one proton from H₂SO₄ gives HSO₄⁻.

quiz.q: The conjugate acid of \(NH_3\) is
quiz.solution: Adding a proton to ammonia gives the ammonium ion.

quiz.q: Which of these is amphiprotic?
quiz.solution: HCO₃⁻ can donate a proton (to CO₃²⁻) or accept one (to H₂CO₃).

quiz.q: The basicity of \(H_3PO_4\) is
quiz.solution: It has three replaceable hydrogen atoms.

quiz.q: Which acid is monobasic?
quiz.solution: HNO₃ has only one replaceable hydrogen.

quiz.q: Strength of an acid refers to its
quiz.solution: Strong acids ionise completely; weak acids partially.

quiz.q: Which is a weak acid?
quiz.solution: Ethanoic acid is only partially ionised in water.

quiz.q: \(K_w\) at 25°C is
quiz.solution: The ionic product of water is 1×10⁻¹⁴ mol²dm⁻⁶.

quiz.q: The pH of 0.001 mol dm⁻³ HCl is
A solution has pOH = 4. Its pH is
The pH of 0.05 mol dm⁻³ \(H_2SO_4\) (fully ionised) is
quiz.solution: [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, so pH = 1.

quiz.q: Phenolphthalein in an alkaline solution is
quiz.solution: It is colourless in acid and pink in alkali.

quiz.q: Methyl orange changes colour over the pH range
quiz.solution: Methyl orange: red at 3.1 to yellow at 4.4.

quiz.q: The best indicator for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide is
quiz.solution: The equivalence pH is above 7, matching phenolphthalein's range.

quiz.q: The best indicator for titrating ammonia with hydrochloric acid is
quiz.solution: The equivalence point is acidic (about pH 5).

quiz.q: A weak acid–weak base titration is not usually performed because
options: there is no sharp pH change at the end-point
quiz.solution: The pH curve has no steep portion, so no indicator gives a sharp end-point.

quiz.q: Which is a suitable primary standard?
quiz.solution: It is pure, stable and non-hygroscopic; NaOH is deliquescent and HCl volatile.

quiz.q: A pipette is used to
quiz.solution: The pipette delivers a fixed volume, usually 20 or 25 cm³.

quiz.q: Concordant titres are readings that agree within about
quiz.solution: Titres within 0.1–0.2 cm³ are averaged.

quiz.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.1 M NaOH exactly neutralised 25.0 cm³ of an acid HX. HX is
quiz.solution: Equal volumes and equal concentrations react 1:1, so HX is monobasic.

quiz.q: 20.0 cm³ of 0.1 M \(H_2SO_4\) neutralises how many moles of NaOH?
quiz.solution: Moles acid = 0.002; ratio 1:2 gives 0.004 mol NaOH.

quiz.q: A salt formed when only part of the replaceable hydrogen is replaced is a
quiz.solution: Examples: NaHSO₄, NaHCO₃.

quiz.q: \(KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot12H_2O\) is an example of a
quiz.solution: Alum ionises to give all constituent ions, so it is a double salt.

quiz.q: Which salt is insoluble in water?
quiz.solution: Barium tetraoxosulphate(VI) is insoluble.

quiz.q: All trioxonitrate(V) salts are
quiz.solution: Nitrates are without exception soluble in water.

quiz.q: The best method for preparing copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) is
quiz.solution: Copper is below hydrogen in the series, so the insoluble-oxide route is used.

quiz.q: Silver chloride is best prepared by
quiz.solution: AgNO₃ + NaCl gives an immediate white precipitate.

quiz.q: A hydrated salt that loses water to the air and crumbles is said to be
quiz.solution: Efflorescence, e.g. Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

quiz.q: Which substance is deliquescent?
quiz.solution: Solid NaOH absorbs enough water to dissolve in it.

quiz.q: Concentrated \(H_2SO_4\) is used in a desiccator because it is
quiz.solution: It absorbs moisture without dissolving, i.e. it is hygroscopic (a drying agent).

quiz.q: The blue colour of \(CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O\) is due to
quiz.solution: Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white and turns blue on hydration.

quiz.q: An aqueous solution of \(NH_4Cl\) is
quiz.solution: It is the salt of a strong acid and a weak base, so it hydrolyses to give H⁺.

quiz.q: An aqueous solution of \(CH_3COONa\) is
quiz.solution: Salt of a weak acid and strong base; the anion hydrolyses to give OH⁻.

quiz.q: Which pair forms an acidic buffer?
quiz.solution: A weak acid with its salt buffers on the acid side.

quiz.q: The main buffer in human blood is the
quiz.solution: H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ holds blood near pH 7.4.

quiz.q: Unpolluted rain water is slightly acidic because of dissolved
quiz.solution: CO₂ forms carbonic acid, giving pH about 5.6.

quiz.q: The principal gases responsible for acid rain are
quiz.solution: They form sulphuric and nitric acids in the atmosphere.

quiz.q: Adding dilute HCl to a solid gives a gas that turns lime water milky. The anion is
quiz.solution: CO₂ is released from a trioxocarbonate(IV).

quiz.q: A white precipitate with \(AgNO_3\)/dilute \(HNO_3\) that dissolves in ammonia indicates
quiz.solution: AgCl is white and dissolves in ammonia solution.

quiz.q: A dirty-green precipitate with NaOH indicates
quiz.solution: Fe(OH)₂ is dirty green; Fe(OH)₃ is reddish-brown.

quiz.q: A white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH suggests
quiz.solution: Lead(II) hydroxide is amphoteric and dissolves in excess alkali.

quiz.q: Warming a salt with NaOH gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue. The cation is
quiz.solution: Ammonia gas is released from ammonium salts.

quiz.q: Which acid is both a dehydrating and an oxidising agent when concentrated?
quiz.solution: Concentrated H₂SO₄ chars sugar and oxidises copper on heating.

quiz.q: Neutralisation is best described as the reaction between
quiz.solution: The essential ionic equation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

quiz.q: Which oxide is amphoteric?
quiz.solution: Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and alkalis.

quiz.q: Baking soda used as an antacid is
quiz.solution: Sodium hydrogentrioxocarbonate(IV) neutralises excess stomach acid.

quiz.q: Calcium hydroxide is added to farmland mainly to
options: raise the pH of acidic soil
quiz.solution: Slaked lime neutralises soil acidity.
